fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Into a Music Quiz
fields.features_subheading: Describe the quiz you want, and Emergent builds the questions, the scoring, and the table every answer lands in.
fields.feature_1:
Questions on the music you name

Name a decade, a genre, or a skill such as reading rhythms, and Emergent drafts multiple-choice questions whose wrong options are of the same kind. Edit any of them by prompt.
fields.feature_2:
Every answer in a table you own

Each answer is saved with the player's name, the question, and whether it was right, in a database you own. Sort by question to find the one the whole room got wrong.
fields.feature_3:
One question per phone screen

Players answer one question per screen, sized for a phone propped on a music stand or a bar table. A link in a newsletter or a QR code on a slide opens the quiz for each player.
fields.feature_4:
Scores, bands, and a reason

The app totals each score and shows the result band you wrote, such as 7 or 8 of 8. Each answer carries one line of explanation, and a wrong guess still teaches the clef.
fields.feature_5:
A recap for the host

When the quiz closes, the app sends the host a recap by email or Slack: the average score, each player's total, and the hardest question. The recap also stays in the app.
fields.feature_6:
Your own domain, or the full code

Run the quiz at your own domain; custom domains are included in Emergent and use credits. Paid plans export the full code to your GitHub repository for a developer to extend.

fields.usecase_heading: How Four Groups Run a Music Quiz
fields.tab_content_1:
One French horn question, missed by 38 of 81

Pell Ridge Middle School's 3 seventh-grade music classes, 81 students in all, take a 12-question instrument families quiz. Every answer lands with the student's name and class. The French horn question was missed by 38 of 81, who placed it with the woodwinds, and it goes back on the board before the concert unit.
fields.tab_content_2:
A one-hit wonder question stumps 10 of the 12 teams

At The Owl and Anchor, 12 teams play a 10-question 90s music round every Thursday, answering on their phones. Answers land under each team's name. A question on a 1997 one-hit wonder stumped 10 of the 12 teams, and The Mixtapes took the round with 9 of 10.
fields.tab_content_3:
Every Sunday, the teacher sees who scored under 5 of 8

Linden Lane Piano Studio sends its 26 students an 8-question theory quiz each week. Every Sunday, the teacher gets an email listing who scored under 5 of 8. This week it named 4 students, all of whom missed the key signature questions, and each gets a second pass at key signatures in the next lesson.
fields.tab_content_4:
371 of 530 listeners miss one Friday question

Marsh Hollow Community Radio posts a 10-question music quiz on its website every Friday. Last week 530 listeners took it, and a recap in the station's Slack named the hardest question: the year a local band cut its first record, missed by 371 of 530. Monday's morning show opens on it.

fields.howto_title: How to Make a Music Quiz
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to make a music quiz with fair questions, sourced answers, and score bands that show what each player should review.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Choose one topic and one crowd
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Ask only what can be checked
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Put a source under each answer
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pick a single focus, such as instrument families or 90s hits, and name who plays it: a seventh-grade class or a Thursday trivia crowd. Put both in the prompt so the questions come out pitched at that group's level.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Favor names, years, symbols, and counts: questions with one right option and three plainly wrong ones. Keep taste questions, like the best album of a decade, for a poll after the round, since no answer key settles them.
fields.howto_step_3_des: A fair choice offers four composers, four years, or four instruments from one family. An option from another era or genre gives the answer away, and a player who rules it out learns nothing.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Under every question, add a line that states the answer and where it comes from, such as an album's liner notes or a music theory text. Shown on the result screen, that line settles an argument at the table.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Decide before launch what 7 or 8 of 8 means and what a score of 3 or lower suggests reviewing. Every possible score should fall into exactly one band, or some player finishes and sees a blank result.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Hand the quiz to 2 people who match the audience, a student or a regular, and watch them play it on a phone. Reword any question either one pauses over, and check that both scores show up in the table.
fields.howto_step_7_des: After the first round, sort the table by question and take the most-missed one into the next lesson or trivia night. Ask it again a few weeks later to see whether the second pass stuck.

faq_plan.a: A music quiz is a set of questions about music, such as notation, composers, or the hits of one decade. Each question has one checkable answer, and the score comes at the end. Teachers use one to review a unit, and trivia hosts and radio stations build rounds from one.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a music quiz?
faq_plan.a: Describe it in one sentence to Emergent's AI survey builder: the topic, how many questions, and who will play. Emergent drafts the questions and the answer key, adds scoring, and sets up a database for every answer. Change any question by prompt, play it once yourself, then share the link.

faq_plan.q: Where do I find music quiz questions and answers I can trust?
faq_plan.a: Write them from sources you can name, like the credits on an album sleeve or a music theory text, and keep the source beside each answer. Trivia lists copied without citations are where wrong answer keys come from. The 8-question quiz on this page names a source under every answer.

faq_plan.q: Can I make a free music quiz for my students?
faq_plan.a: Yes. A free music quiz for one class fits on Emergent's free tier, which covers building and publishing. Share the quiz by link or a QR code on the board, and every student's answers collect in one table.

faq_plan.q: How do I build a music quiz that guesses someone's taste?
faq_plan.hint: What is my taste in music quiz?
faq_plan.a: Use a matching quiz instead of a scored one. Each answer points to a result, such as a genre or an era, and the result with the most points wins. Ask about habits, like what plays on a long drive, and word each result as a leaning, never a verdict on the player.

faq_plan.q: How do I write who-am-I music quiz questions about a musician?
faq_plan.hint: Who am i music quiz questions?
faq_plan.a: Write 3 or 4 clues about one artist or composer, starting with the least known fact and ending with the most famous one, then ask players to name the person. Award more points for an early guess, and show each clue on its own screen so nobody reads ahead.

faq_plan.q: How long should a music quiz be?
faq_plan.a: Ten questions fit a trivia round or a weekly listener quiz, and 8 suits a quick theory check-in between lessons. A class review can run 12 to 15 so every topic in the unit appears. Keep a phone round short enough to finish in about 5 minutes.

faq_plan.q: How do I score a music quiz when players answer in groups?
faq_plan.a: Give one point per right answer and save each answer under the team's name, not each player's. Lock answers when the host closes the question, and break ties with one extra question, such as the year a song charted. Emergent puts no cap on responses.

faq_plan.q: What makes a good music quiz for kids?
faq_plan.a: Short questions, 3 options instead of 4, and topics kids can hear or see, like instrument families or the notes on a staff. Write result messages that name what a kid got right first. Read each question aloud once, and split any that takes two breaths to say.

faq_plan.q: Should a music quiz show the right answer after each question?
faq_plan.a: It depends on the setting. In a class, show the answer and one line of explanation right away, while the wrong guess is still fresh. In a trivia round, hold every answer until the round closes; that keeps tables from passing answers to each other.

quiz.title: Music Quiz: 8 Questions on Notes, Instruments, and Composers
quiz.intro: Eight questions on the staff, the orchestra, the piano, and two famous composers. Pick one answer for each; your score and a source for every answer show at the end.

questions.text: How many lines does a standard music staff have?
questions.explanation: A staff is a set of horizontal lines, usually five, with spaces between them. Each line and each space stands for a different pitch.

source.quote: is a set of horizontal lines (usually five) with spaces between them

questions.text: The oboe belongs to which instrument family?
questions.explanation: The oboe is a double-reed woodwind. Oboes are usually made of wood, though some are made of plastic or resin.

source.quote: is a type of double-reed woodwind instrument

questions.text: How many keys does a standard modern piano have?
questions.explanation: A modern piano has 52 white keys and 36 black keys, 88 in all. Some older pianos stop at 85.

source.quote: 52 white keys and 36 black keys, for a total of 88 keys

questions.text: The Ode to Joy closes the Ninth Symphony of which composer?
questions.explanation: Beethoven wrote the Ninth between 1822 and 1824, and it was his final complete symphony.

source.quote: the final complete symphony by Ludwig van Beethoven, composed between 1822 and 1824

questions.text: Who composed The Stars and Stripes Forever, the national march of the United States?
questions.explanation: John Philip Sousa wrote the march in 1896. An act of Congress made it the official national march in 1987.

source.quote: is an American patriotic march written and composed by John Philip Sousa in 1896

questions.text: A note vibrates at 440 Hz. What is the frequency of the note one octave above it?
questions.explanation: An octave up doubles the frequency, so 440 Hz becomes 880 Hz, and an octave down halves it to 220 Hz.

source.quote: if one note has a frequency of 440 Hz, the note one octave above is at 880 Hz

questions.text: How many strings does a standard guitar typically have?
questions.explanation: A guitar typically has 6 strings. The 12-string guitar doubles them into 6 pairs.

source.quote: typically has six or twelve strings

questions.text: The treble clef is also known as which clef?
questions.explanation: The treble clef is the G clef: it sits on the second line of the staff and fixes that line as the G above middle C.

source.quote: the treble clef, also known as the G clef, is placed on the second line
